title: Essence and Existence in Arabic and Islamic Philosophy

summaries.example: Think about a triangle drawn on paper. Its essence is what makes it a triangle: it has three sides. Its existence is the fact that this particular triangle is actually on the paper. You can understand what a triangle is even before checking whether one has been drawn.
summaries.summary: Arabic and Islamic philosophers explored the difference between a thing’s essence—what it is—and its existence—the fact that it is real. Early thinkers did not all separate these ideas. Some kalām thinkers held that things could have a kind of status before being created, while Ashʿarite thinkers emphasized that things depend fully on God. Avicenna made the distinction central: we can understand “horse” or “triangle” without knowing whether one exists. He also taught that created things depend on another cause for existence, while God is the Necessary Existent. Later thinkers challenged or revised his view. Some said essence and existence are different ideas but not two separate things in reality. Others, especially Mullā Ṣadrā, treated existence as the basic reality and essences as ways the mind organizes it.
key_ideas: Philosophers asked whether what a thing is differs from the fact that it exists.
Some thinkers said this difference is only a difference in our thoughts. Others said it reflects a difference in reality.
Avicenna argued that we can understand what something is without knowing whether it exists.
Later philosophers disagreed about whether essences or existence is more basic.
These debates also raised questions about God, creation, and whether essences depend on God.
summaries.why_it_matters: This debate helps explain how philosophers think about reality, imagination, definitions, and creation. It also shows that a single question can connect many topics: what things are, how we know them, and how they depend on causes. Learning about the debate introduces children to the idea that thoughtful people can disagree about deep questions while giving reasons for their views.

important_terms.definition: What a thing is: the features that make it the kind of thing it is.
The fact that something is real or present, rather than only imagined.
The study of what is real and what it means for something to be real.
A philosophical tradition in the Islamic world influenced by Greek philosophy.
A tradition of Islamic theology and philosophy that developed its own questions and ideas.
The philosopher Ibn Sīnā, whose ideas strongly shaped later discussions of essence and existence.

questions_to_think_about: Can you describe what a unicorn is without believing that unicorns are real?
Is a difference in our ideas always a difference in the world itself?
If something is imagined, does it exist in any sense?
Which seems more basic: the kind of thing something is, or the fact that it is there?

summaries.example: Consider the number four. We can understand that four is even without asking whether four physical objects are currently in front of us. Avicenna used examples like this to argue that what something is can be understood apart from whether it exists. He therefore distinguished essence from existence, while also holding that essences do not exist as independent objects before they are instantiated in the world or in the mind.
summaries.summary: The entry follows a long debate in Arabic and Islamic philosophy about whether a thing’s essence—its nature or what-it-is—is distinct from its existence. Early falsafa, including al-Kindī and al-Fārābī, did not straightforwardly endorse the later Avicennan distinction. Classical kalām developed competing accounts: Basran Muʿtazilites gave things a status beyond their existence and treated being existent as a special non-entitative state, whereas Ashʿarites denied that things have reality before creation and rejected a separate existence-predicate. Avicenna argued from conceivability: since we can know what a human, horse, or triangle is without knowing whether it exists, existence is extrinsic to essence. Yet he did not treat essences as independently real before existence. His account includes mental existence, the Necessary Existent, and an analogy or modulation of existence that distinguishes divine from created existence without making the concept wholly equivocal or univocal. Later thinkers often accepted a conceptual distinction while rejecting a real one, partly because separating essence and existence seems to create regress problems. Others defended realism by denying that existence is an entity like a quality. In later metaphysics, al-Suhrawardī is associated with primacy of essence, while Mullā Ṣadrā argues for primacy of existence and an existence-centered form of ontological monism.
key_ideas: The central question is whether essence and existence are distinct, and, if so, whether the distinction is real or merely conceptual.
Al-Fārābī analyzed existence in more than one sense, while early falsafa generally avoided a clear metaphysical separation between essence and existence.
Basran Muʿtazilites allowed things a status beyond their existence and described being existent as a non-entitative state; Ashʿarites rejected such a separation.
Avicenna’s conceivability test holds that if we can understand what something is without knowing that it exists, existence is not essential to its essence.
Avicenna maintained that created things are contingent in themselves but necessary through their causes, whereas God alone is Necessary Existent in Itself.
Post-Avicennan thinkers debated conceptualism and realism, and later metaphysics divided between primacy of essence and primacy of existence.
summaries.why_it_matters: The debate is important because it links definitions, language, thought, and reality. It asks whether a conceptual difference can justify a metaphysical conclusion, and it examines what it means for something to depend on a cause. The discussion also shaped Islamic accounts of God, creation, necessity, possibility, and the status of imagined objects. Studying its changes over time reveals both continuity and disagreement within Islamic philosophy rather than a single fixed position.

important_terms.definition: The nature, definition, or “what-it-is” of something; in this debate it is considered separately from whether the thing exists.
The actuality or presence of a thing; Arabic philosophers commonly discussed it using the term wujūd.
The philosophical study of being, reality, and what kinds of things there are.
The Islamic philosophical tradition shaped by Greek Aristotelian and Neoplatonic sources translated into Arabic.
A parallel Islamic theological-philosophical tradition with distinctive theories about creation, entities, and attributes.
Ibn Sīnā, whose analysis of essence and existence became a framework for much later Islamic metaphysics.
The view that essence and existence differ in meaning but do not name two independently existing entities outside the mind.
The view that essence and existence have a distinction in reality, not merely in thought or language.

questions_to_think_about: Does the ability to define or imagine something without knowing that it exists prove a distinction in reality?
What problems arise if essence and existence are treated as two separate entities joined together?
How does mental existence help explain thoughts about fictional or nonexistent objects?
Why might a philosopher prefer primacy of essence, while another prefers primacy of existence?
Can something be contingent in itself yet necessary when considered together with its causes?

summaries.example: Imagine a dragon in a story. You can explain what a dragon is supposed to be without claiming that a real dragon exists. This supports the idea that “what it is” and “whether it is real” are different questions. But philosophers still have to ask whether the dragon’s essence exists somewhere—in the world, only in your mind, or not as a thing at all.
summaries.summary: This entry studies a major debate in Arabic and Islamic philosophy: is a thing’s essence, or what it is, different from its existence, or the fact that it is real? The question appeared in several traditions. Early falsafa often treated being and what a thing is as closely connected. Basran Muʿtazilite thinkers argued that things could have a kind of reality or “thing-ness” before creation, while Ashʿarite thinkers said that things depend completely on God and have no reality before God creates them. Avicenna offered a highly influential analysis. We can understand a horse or triangle without knowing whether one exists, so essence and existence differ conceptually. He also held that created things depend on causes for their existence, while God is the Necessary Existent. Avicenna’s theory of mental existence explains how we can think about things that are not outside the mind. After him, many philosophers accepted a difference in meaning but denied that essence and existence are two separate objects in reality. Others defended a real distinction through ideas such as the non-entitativity of existence. Later debates contrasted primacy of essence, associated with thinkers such as al-Suhrawardī, with primacy of existence, associated especially with Mullā Ṣadrā.
key_ideas: Philosophers disagreed about whether things have any status before they exist.
Basran Muʿtazilites and Ashʿarites offered different accounts of creation and reality.
Avicenna argued that essence and existence can be understood separately, but he did not simply make essences independent objects.
Later philosophers criticized the idea that essence and existence are two separate parts, because this can lead to an endless question about whether each part exists.
Some later thinkers defended a real distinction; others treated existence as a mental or conceptual notion.
Mullā Ṣadrā later argued that existence is primary and that distinct essences are ways reality appears to us.
summaries.why_it_matters: The issue matters because it connects everyday questions about definitions and imagined objects with difficult questions about reality and God. It also shows why philosophical arguments need careful distinctions. Two people may agree that the words “horse” and “exists” mean different things but disagree about whether that difference exists outside the mind. Following the debate helps us see how ideas develop through criticism, revision, and new systems.

important_terms.definition: What a thing is, such as being a horse, triangle, or human being.
The fact that a thing is real or has an instance outside the mind.
The branch of philosophy that studies being, reality, and what kinds of things exist.
An Islamic philosophical tradition influenced by Aristotle and Neoplatonism through Arabic translations.
An Islamic theological and philosophical tradition that developed alongside falsafa.
The name commonly used for Ibn Sīnā, the philosopher who made this distinction central.
A view that existence is mainly a concept applied to things we understand, not a separate thing in the world.
A view that essence and existence are distinct in reality, not only in our thinking.

questions_to_think_about: If you can describe a fictional creature, does that creature exist in your mind?
Should something be called real only if it exists outside the mind?
Why might attaching existence to an essence create an endless chain of further existences?
What would the world look like if existence were primary and kinds such as “horse” and “human” were only mental divisions?
